promise: Repeal the Foreshore and Seabed Act 2004 and restore Māori access to the courts for customary title
made: Founding kaupapa (2004); 2008 National–Māori Party confidence and supply agreement
detail: The party was founded over this issue. In the 2008 agreement National committed only to review the 2004 Act. The Marine and Coastal Area (Takutai Moana) Act 2011 replaced it and passed 63–56, supported by National, the Māori Party and United Future. Labour, the Greens, ACT and Hone Harawira voted against. The new Act restored the right to go to court for customary title. Tariana Turia backed it while calling it 'drafted by politics, rather than what is fair and moral'. Harawira quit the party over the compromise and formed Mana. In October 2025 the National-led government's amendment raised the legal test for customary marine title. Te Pāti Māori opposed it, and its MPs burned a copy outside Parliament.

promise: Protect (and entrench) the Māori electorates
detail: National had campaigned on abolishing the Māori seats. In the 2008 agreement it promised not to remove them 'without the consent of the Māori people', and it kept that promise. The seats still exist in 2026. Entrenchment, the Māori Party's own aim, was shelved: both parties agreed they would 'not be pursuing the entrenchment of the Māori seats this parliamentary term'.

promise: A review of constitutional arrangements, including Māori representation
detail: The review began in 2011 as a commitment under the agreement. We found no evidence in this pass that it led to significant constitutional change. Te Pāti Māori's 2026 programme (Mātike Mai, a Te Tiriti Commission, a 2040 target) shows the party sees this as unfinished business.

promise: Whānau Ora: whānau-centred, Māori-led delivery of health and social services
made: 2008 agreement (Turia's flagship); made a cornerstone of the 2011 agreement
detail: Announced in April 2010 with Turia as Minister for Whānau Ora. Three commissioning agencies were set up in 2014. It is the party's most lasting policy achievement. Critics, including Winston Peters, said its outcomes were hard to measure and that funding was concentrated in Turia's electorate. In 2025 the National-led government re-tendered the contracts, and the Whānau Ora Commissioning Agency, led by party president John Tamihere, lost its contract. Te Puni Kōkiri also ordered a review into whether Whānau Ora money had been used for 'electioneering', namely an advertising campaign urging Māori to join the Māori roll.

promise: New Zealand to support the UN Declaration on the Rights of Indigenous Peoples (UNDRIP)
made: Māori Party policy; secured during the 2008–11 term
detail: Pita Sharples, as Māori Affairs Minister, announced New Zealand's support at the UN Permanent Forum on 20 April 2010. Under Labour in 2007, New Zealand had been one of four countries to vote against the declaration. Sharples credited the National–Māori Party relationship. Support was for a 'non-binding' declaration. Making UNDRIP enforceable remains a 2026 Te Pāti Māori goal.

promise: Cut smoking (Turia's tobacco agenda): higher tobacco excise, plain packaging, Smokefree 2025
detail: In 2011 the government adopted a Smokefree 2025 goal, with steep excise increases and later plain packaging, all led by Turia. A separate Labour smokefree-generation law (2022) was repealed by the National-led government in February 2024, which Te Pāti Māori opposed.

promise: A new Māori language law giving Māori a stronger role in revitalising te reo
made: 2014 confidence and supply term (Te Ururoa Flavell as Minister for Māori Development)
detail: Te Ture mō Te Reo Māori 2016 (the Māori Language Act 2016) set up Te Mātāwai to act for iwi and Māori on language revitalisation. It was enacted in both te reo Māori and English, a first for New Zealand.

promise: Reform Māori land law (Te Ture Whenua Māori Bill)
detail: Flavell's bill was introduced in 2016. It proved controversial and did not pass before the 2017 election. The new Labour minister withdrew it. Smaller targeted amendments passed in 2020.

promise: Recognition of the New Zealand Wars
detail: A national day of commemoration for the New Zealand Wars began in 2017 and is held on 28 October. It followed a 2015 petition from Ōtorohanga College students. After the 2017 defeat, Marama Fox credited Flavell with this, with the pardon of Rua Kenana, and with UNDRIP support. The Māori Party was one of several actors involved.

promise: Win back the Māori electorates through an electoral pact with Mana (2017)
made: February 2017 (the Māori Party stood aside in Te Tai Tokerau for Hone Harawira)
detail: Labour won all seven Māori seats in 2017. Flavell lost Waiariki, and the party left Parliament on 1.18% of the party vote. Metro magazine and others put the defeat down to a backlash against nine years of supporting National.

promise: An independent Māori Health Authority
detail: Te Pāti Māori was not in government, but Labour created Te Aka Whai Ora, a Māori Health Authority, in its 2022 health reforms. The National-led government abolished it under urgency on 28 February 2024. The 2026 platform promises 'investment in Māori health outcomes'.

promise: No coalition with the right (National/ACT)
detail: This reversed the party's 2008–17 approach of working with National. Te Pāti Māori stayed in opposition after 2023. In 2026 it is asking supporters to give their electorate vote to Te Pāti Māori and their party vote to Labour or the Greens, to remove the coalition.

promise: Disclose political donations as the law requires
detail: In April 2021 the Electoral Commission referred the party to Police for failing to disclose about $320,000 of donations in time. They included $158,224 from then co-leader John Tamihere and $120,000 from Aotearoa Te Kahu LP. Police passed the case to the Serious Fraud Office, which closed it in 2022 without charges. The party blamed volunteers who did not know the rules. In 2022 Charities Services also examined loans and payments to Tamihere's 2020 campaigns from charities he leads (Te Whānau o Waipareira Trust, NUMA).

promise: Stand candidates in general (non-Māori) electorates at the 2026 election
detail: By October 2026 the party was standing only seven candidates, one in each Māori electorate. Its party list has one name, party secretary Lance Norman. This fits its strategic-voting call, but it reverses the 2025 announcement.

promise: Contest all seven Māori electorates in 2026
detail: Candidates are standing in all seven seats, including Aperahama Edwards in Te Tai Tokerau and Lisa Marie Murch in Te Tai Tonga. Those two electorate committees had resigned in support of Kapa-Kingi and Ferris. The party is up against two of its own former MPs: Kapa-Kingi (Te Tai Tokerau Party) and Tākuta Ferris (independent).

promise: A Parliamentary Commissioner for Te Tiriti with power to audit and veto non-compliant bills, as a coalition 'bottom line'
detail: Labour's Chris Hipkins said he would not support a commissioner able to overturn laws, though he was open to better 'checks and balances'. The 2026 package of 1 September 2026 proposes an independent Te Tiriti Commission to investigate Crown breaches, binding Waitangi Tribunal recommendations, a 2040 constitutional-reform target and a $200m Mātike Mai fund. Labour has ruled out the Commission and Mātike Mai. We found no 2026 source confirming whether the veto power or the 'bottom line' status still stands.

promise: Abolish prisons by 2040 in favour of community-led solutions
detail: Labour said it was 'dead-set against' the policy.

promise: 'Kiwi Tax Plan': a 48% rate on income over $300,000, a rebate for people earning under $30,000, a wealth tax, a higher company tax rate, land-banking and vacant-home taxes, a 5% stamp duty and no GST on kai
made: 2026 election (26 August 2026); largely repeats the 2023 tax plan
detail: This is very close to the 2023 package (zero tax under $30,000, 48% over $300,000, 33% company tax, a wealth tax, GST off food), which shows consistency over time. None of it was enacted in 2023–26, when the party was in opposition.

promise: A $1 billion fund for Māori and community ownership of new renewable energy ('energy sovereignty')
Give Māori collectives Crown-owned land and $100m to set up supermarket chains
A $200m Takatāpui Commission
detail: RNZ reported the pledge as '$200 million to change who holds power for decisions about takatāpui' (Māori LGBTQ+ people). Check the exact powers proposed in the party's policy document.
